title: [CLO Beginner's Guide] Materials_Deep Dive_Understanding CLO Fabrics
description:
CLO Beginner's Guide, Material-Related Series Courses. Understand CLO fabrics and master the methods of representing garment materials, including buttons, textures, interlinings, bindings, zippers, topstitching, sewing wrinkles, and hardware accessories. This course will take you deep into learning how to skillfully use CLO materials.  
Course references:  
【Designer’s CLO Journey | 3D Design and Production of Spring/Summer Printed Dress】 【Jump directly to 1:16:20】 https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1Fm4y1a7U7/?share_source=copy_web&vd_source=8fa0498188fde5bf10ad19975ecc4a3f&t=4580  
【CLO 2025.1 - CLOFAB】 https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1RMHrzyEr6?spm_id_from=333.788.videopod.sections&vd_source=9c04d674e69dc88a344e06b67b3bdf39
transcript:
In the last course, we gained a basic understanding of CLO fabric.  
In this course, we will study CLO fabric in more depth.  
First, let's get to know the 3D stickers and PBR stickers under the fabric texture attribute.  
In 3D software, the physical visual effect of an object is usually expressed by using different PBR stickers.  
Each sticker represents a visual texture attribute.  
In CLO, you can use these six stickers:  
Structure map, bump map, normal map, transparency map, surface roughness map, and metalness map.  
When these stickers are used together, the texture becomes more complete and realistic.  

The first one is the structure map.  
Through the structure map, the color or print of the fabric is displayed in 3D.  
It is the most important sticker to express the texture’s visual effect.  

The bump map is the second most important sticker, similar to the structure map.  
Through the bump map, the fine details of the fabric are displayed,  
such as edge structure, wrinkles, etc.  
The bump map only enhances the visual effect of rough details.  
From a side view, the surface still appears smooth.  

The normal map can show the actual roughness of the fabric surface.  
This map is a grayscale image.  
The closer to the black area, the closer to the bottom of the material.  
The closer to the white area, the closer to the material surface.  
This image also represents the surface of the material.  
In some cases, the normal map will add a high-definition blur  
to smooth the edges of the shapes.  

The transparency map defines the degree of transparency and translucency on certain areas of the fabric surface.  
In CLO, there are two different sticker modes to express material transparency: RGB and Alpha.  
The RGB mode uses a grayscale image with no transparency channel.  
The closer the area is to white, the less transparent it is; the closer to black, the more transparent it is.  
The depth of the gray scale determines the degree of transparency.  
In Alpha mode, images in .png, .tif, or .psd formats are used.  
The alpha channel value reflects the transparency effect.  

The surface roughness map controls the light reflection information on the fabric surface, thereby expressing the surface roughness.  
This sticker is a grayscale map.  
The closer to black, the more reflected light.  
The closer to white, the less reflected light.  

The metalness map defines the areas on the fabric surface with metallic characteristics.  
The sticker is a black-and-white image.  
The black area represents non-metal materials.  
The white area represents metal materials.  
In CLO, the user can set the surface roughness and metalness,  
then combine the metalness map to express the metallic effect on the fabric surface.  

How to obtain a seamless PBR sticker?  
Method 1: Use a regular scanner, such as Canon, Epson, etc.  
Scan the texture and process the seams to get a seamless texture.  
Use Photoshop software to generate other PBR stickers.  

Method 2: Use a professional scanner.  
Use professional scanners, such as WeZoo, Revolvet, etc.  
With professional pattern processing software,  
you can scan, process, and automatically generate various PBR stickers more efficiently.  

Next, I will take you through comprehensive practice with digital fabrics in CLO.  
Open the library, select CLO Training, search for materials,  
find materials, and learn more about CLO fabric documents.  
Double-click to open.  
You will see that this is a solid file using a default fabric.  
Close the library window.  

Next, we will add the corresponding maps to complete the PBR stickers.  
In the Object window, select Material 1.  
In the Attribute Editor displayed below,  
there are corresponding add-on slots for the texture, bump map, and normal map, etc.  
There are four small square icons on the right side of each sticker column.  
Add the corresponding stickers through them.  
In the Object window, click the four small square icons.  
Select the object.  
Double-click to open in the bottom right.  
At this time, a message will pop up.  
Click OK.  
You can add all PBR stickers at once.  
Press Confirm.  
Add the object again.  
Click OK.  
Only add the selected object.  
If you want to add all stickers at once,  
click Confirm.  

Note that each PBR sticker needs to be named according to the material name rules.  
All PBR images should be placed in a folder.  
Each PBR sticker has a corresponding add-on name,  
as shown on the screen.  

When adding a texture,  
CLO can automatically create a bump map.  
There is an auto-create button on the right.  
Click it.  
It will automatically create a bump map.  

When adding a texture,  
the other five PBR stickers, such as the bump map, normal map, and transparency map,  
can also be created using the auto-create button.  
If the material already has a bump map,  
open the library window,  
go to My Library.  
Open the first folder of the five materials.  
Add the bump map.  
At the bottom, adjust the bump map strength;  
the larger the value,  
the more prominent the details on the fabric.  
If the value is negative,  
the visual effect of the auto-create will be reversed.  
Now drag the bump map to the bump map slot.  

There is a set of parameters at the bottom  
used to control the three-dimensional effect of the texture surface.  
Let's understand the meaning of each parameter.  

The Height Range adjusts the maximum height of the fabric surface.  
If the input value is 3,  
the white area will display a maximum height of 3 mm,  
and the black area will display a maximum height of 5 mm.  

Offset adjusts the distance between the 3D grid and the fabric surface.  
Height Cutoff can cut off the decal height below the set height of the grid.  

Particle Size adjusts the particle size of the 3D grid.  
The smaller the particle size,  
the more details can be displayed.  
At the same time, the file size will increase.  
Rendering time will also be longer.  

To maintain continuity,  
you can open and remove the border line of the adjacent surface.  

After understanding each parameter,  
set the Height Range to 3,  
Particle Size to 1.  

To preview and check the effect of the changes,  
open the render window,  
press the render button.  
You can see the fabric surface has three-dimensional details.  
After checking, stop rendering  
and close the render window.  

Drag the transparency map from the folder into the window.  
Keep the mode as RGB.  
Open the surface of the dense texture.  
You can see the fabric in 3D has a hollow effect.  

The surface roughness map,  
the small right-pointing triangle,  
has two options: Intensity and Map.  
When Intensity is selected,  
the larger the value,  
the rougher the surface.  

Adjusting Reflection Intensity  
expresses the material’s gloss effect.  
The larger the value,  
the glossier the surface.  

Adjusting Metal Density  
applies the metal effect  
to the entire material.  
The larger the value,  
the stronger the metal effect.  

Change the option to Map.  
Drag the surface roughness texture into it.  
Reduce Intensity to 65.  
Reduce Reflection Intensity to 90.  

The default black area is a fully reflective area.  
If the black and white areas are reversed,  
you can select the opposite direction.  

Finally, add the metalness map.  
Set Metal Density to 100.  
The metal effect will be fully displayed.  

In the render window,  
you can see the final effect  
of the glass material.  

After completing the material,  
it can be saved locally  
so it can be dragged and used directly next time.  

In the Property Editor,  
enter the material name, structure, and other information in the Info area.  
Click Save.  

In CLO,  
you can use the material editor  
to design and edit PBR images separately.  

First, open the material from the picture library Connect.  
Select Free and Official Accounts.  
Find a fabric with a blue-white gradient.  
Double-click to add it to the Object window.  
Apply it to the board.  
Select this material in the Object window.  
In the Property Editor,  
click the three dots next to the material image.  
Open the material editor.  

First, let's learn about the interface layout of the material editor.  
At the top,  
Width and Height define the size of the image.  
Click the triangle on the right of the pixel value.  
The size unit for setting the image can be changed.  
PPI is used to set the image resolution.  
Click this icon.  
You can set whether the image is transparent.  
Click the preview settings button on the right.  
You can choose to display or hide the grid.  
The Circular Opacity controls the opacity of the repeated image.  
Reset restores the default settings.  

At the bottom left of the material editor and in the layer list,  
you can set layers.  
The currently displayed layer is the fabric’s material image.  
Click the add icon to add a new layer.  
Click the select icon to select layers.  
You can also duplicate, lock, delete, and select layers.  
If there are multiple layers,  
you can drag and drop them to adjust their stacking order.  
Click the icon on the left of the pixel value  
to show or hide this layer.  
The name of the double layer can be changed or renamed.  

After selecting a layer,  
you can edit the image properties of the selected layer.  
Layer blending can mix the selected layer with the underlying layer  
in a chosen mode.  
Colors can be set for the image.  
Color Switching can change colors of different areas,  
using the current blue and white pattern.  
Click Color Switch.  
Enter the number of colors in this pattern, 2.  
Purple and blue display two color blocks.  
Hover the mouse over a color block.  
Its corresponding position highlights in bright yellow.  
Click the first color block.  
Set the color to black.  
Set the second color block to red.  
Click Apply.  
The new image will replace the original pattern.  

Apply it to the fabric.  
Click the saved image in the lower left corner.  
The new pattern can be saved in the local file library.  

The pattern editor has not yet been used.  

The 3D design and production of spring and summer prints in CLO  
allow you to comment and click in the comment area.  
You can print the design onto the fabric surface.  
Click the three dots on the right side of the fabric.  
Open the print image; it will be added underneath this material.  
Select the print in the Attribute Editor, and enter print information as required.  

Under Environment Settings, you can set the print display surface: front, back, or both.  
You can also set the print repeat type: flat, horizontal offset, vertical offset, etc.  

Additionally, you can select a PBR sticker that uses the same PBR as the material.  
The PBR stickers of each material can be automatically applied to the print,  
allowing the print and fabric to harmoniously integrate and present a more realistic and coordinated visual effect.  

You can also use the same image and material in each sticker,  
and selectively apply a specific sticker.  

Change the print type to metal.  
This lets the print display a metal effect.  

The print is the most important part of the pattern.  
The final effect is completed.  

Save the entire fabric as a ZFAB file.  
You can also save the print attributes.  

In addition to the physical appearance of the fabric,  
there is also a physical attribute that determines the fabric’s texture,  
and its stretch and expansion characteristics.  

How to obtain the physical attributes of fabric in CLO?  
First, CLO software includes more than 70 physical fabric attributes.  
You can apply them directly.  
Select the fabric in the Object window.  
At the bottom of the Attribute Editor, find the Physical Attribute section.  
The physical attributes are displayed on the right side.  
Click the triangle next to the preview.  
This shows all built-in fabric physical attributes in the software.  
Click the physical attribute for the fabric to apply it.  
Click Details below.  
The selected physical attribute detail parameters will be displayed.  

Let's understand the core parameters together.  

Tensile Strength and Corner Line Strength  
indicate the fabric’s stretch performance.  
The larger the value, the harder the fabric is to stretch,  
such as denim, plain cotton, etc.  
The smaller the value, the easier the fabric stretches,  
such as knitted fabric, thin silk, etc.  

Fabric hardness is controlled by bending strength.  
The larger the number, the stiffer the fabric,  
like denim and leather.  
The lower the number, the softer the fabric,  
like silk and soft flannel.  

In the preview, select denim.  
It is difficult to observe fabric wrinkles.  
Switch to thick white fabric.  
Select the Sichuan simulation.  
You can see the fabric surface in the 3D window.  
It wrinkles easily and is considered stiff.  

If you choose the knitted fabric simulation,  
you can see the fabric surface is smooth  
and the feel is softer.  

The deformation value is used to indicate the shape of fabric wrinkles.  

Now I am demonstrating CLO’s V1 fabric.  
When new users use the new version of CLO,  
only V2 fabric is available.  

In the physical property details,  
V2 fabric has a higher growth rate than V1 fabric.  
Growth rate is used to accurately capture  
the nonlinear stretching behavior of real objects,  
improving simulation and scroll accuracy.  

In the Property Editor,  
pull down the menu.  
You can see weight, friction coefficient, and thickness of the fabric.  

In the software, besides fabrics,  
there are also physical property presets for elastic bands.  
Open the small triangle next to fabric.  
Select elastic band.  
The presets include needle elastic band and shrink elastic band.  
You can choose according to your needs.  

Besides the physical properties built into the software,  
we can also use the CLO fabric measuring device  
to measure fabric  
and obtain accurate physical properties.  

Like the new fabric measuring device shown on the right in the picture,  
the CLO Z-FAB Kit,  
which significantly improves automation and accuracy.  

The CLOF app tool in the software  
helps us quickly and accurately digitize fabrics.  

Let me give you a brief introduction.  
The CLOF app tool in the software  
can be opened in three ways.  

If you want to create a new fabric from scratch,  
click the Object window.  
At the top of the fabric list, click CLOF app.  
You will create a new fabric after clicking.  

If you want to modify texture and physical properties of existing fabrics,  
click the three small dots on the right side of the fabric.  
Select Physical Properties to start the CLOF app.  

You can also click a single blue fabric in the main menu,  
then click CLOF app in the purple menu.  
You can start creating new fabrics.  

The CLOF app window will pop up in the 2D window area.  
You can switch between the CLOF app and the 2D window.  

At the top of the CLOF app window,  
you can enter the fabric name, supplier, and other information.  

Next is the preview area.  
You can click the link here  
to open the CLOF app related manual for learning.  

Below are the physical properties settings.  
The basic workflow is to create a physical pattern first,  
then set physical properties.  

When creating a fabric physical pattern under physical properties,  
if you have the CLOF Z-FAB Kit scanning device,  
you can click the first option.  

If you do not have the device,  
but have scanned image files from other devices,  
you can click to open the image.  
In the open file window,  
select the scanned image file,  
then proceed with the physical pattern operation.  

If the scanned image file follows the specified file naming rules,  
the CLOF app can automatically upload  
PBR stickers within the same folder.  

Click Physical Properties.  
You can create fabric physical properties in this interface.  

There is a switch menu for the CLOF Z-FAB fabric scroll test device on the right.  
If you have the CLOF Z-FAB fabric scroll test device,  
click Use.  

If you do not have the device,  
you can also select the fabric type,  
enter fiber content percentage,  
weight, and thickness information,  
to quickly and easily create suitable fabric physical properties for clothing.  

If you want to learn how to use the CLOF Z-FAB tool in detail  
to create physical and physical properties of digital fabrics,  
you can click on the video link in the comment section  
for further study.

chunks.content: # CLO Beginner's Guide: Materials Deep Dive – Understanding CLO Fabrics This document provides a detailed overview of CLO fabric textures, PBR stickers, material editing, physical fabric attributes, and the use of CLO's fabric measuring tools. It covers technical terms such as structure map, bump map, normal map, transparency map, surface roughness map, metalness map, PBR (Physically Based Rendering), and CLOF Z-FAB Kit for fabric digitization. --- ## PBR Stickers in CLO Fabric Texturing This section explains the six key PBR stickers used in CLO to enhance fabric realism and visual effects, detailing their functions and how they contribute to fabric appearance. - **Structure Map**: Displays the color or print of the fabric in 3D; the most critical sticker for visual texture. - **Bump Map**: Shows fine surface details like wrinkles and edges; enhances roughness visually but does not alter the smooth side view. - **Normal Map**: A grayscale image representing actual fabric surface height variations; black areas correspond to lower points, white to surface peaks. Sometimes includes a blur for smoothing edges. - **Transparency Map**: Defines fabric transparency/translucency in two modes: - **RGB mode**: Grayscale image without alpha channel; white means opaque, black means transparent. - **Alpha mode**: Uses image formats (.png, .tif, .psd) with alpha channel controlling transparency. - **Surface Roughness Map**: Controls light reflection on the fabric; grayscale where black reflects more light and white reflects less. - **Metalness Map**: Defines metallic areas; black is non-metal, white is metal. Combined with surface roughness to simulate metallic fabric effects. --- ## Creating Seamless PBR Stickers Two main methods to obtain seamless PBR stickers for CLO fabrics: 1. **Regular Scanners (e.g., Canon, Epson)** - Scan fabric textures, manually process seams in Photoshop, generate PBR stickers. 2. **Professional Scanners (e.g., WeZoo, Revolvet)** - Use specialized pattern processing software for automatic scanning and generation of PBR stickers with higher efficiency. --- ## Applying PBR Stickers in CLO Instructions for adding PBR stickers to fabric materials in CLO: - Open the Object window and select the material. - Use four small square icons next to each texture slot (texture, bump map, normal map, etc.) to add stickers. - Add all stickers at once by confirming the prompt or add selectively. - PBR sticker files must be named according to CLO’s material naming conventions and stored in a single folder. - CLO can **auto-create bump maps** (and other PBR maps) from base textures via an "auto-create" button. - Adjust bump map strength in the Attribute Editor; positive values enhance detail prominence, negative values invert the effect. --- ## Key Parameters for 3D Texture Effects Parameters controlling the 3D texture surface effects include: - **Height Range**: Maximum height of fabric surface peaks and valleys (e.g., white area = 3 mm height, black area = 5 mm depth). - **Offset**: Distance between the 3D grid and fabric surface. - **Height Cutoff**: Clips decal height below a threshold.

chunks.content: - Adjust bump map strength in the Attribute Editor; positive values enhance detail prominence, negative values invert the effect. --- ## Key Parameters for 3D Texture Effects Parameters controlling the 3D texture surface effects include: - **Height Range**: Maximum height of fabric surface peaks and valleys (e.g., white area = 3 mm height, black area = 5 mm depth). - **Offset**: Distance between the 3D grid and fabric surface. - **Height Cutoff**: Clips decal height below a threshold. - **Particle Size**: Size of particles in the 3D grid; smaller particles show more detail but increase file size and render time. - **Border Line Removal**: Ensures continuity by removing adjacent surface borders. Recommended settings for preview: Height Range = 3, Particle Size = 1. --- ## Previewing Fabric Effects in CLO - Use the render window to preview 3D textures and fabric details. - Drag and drop transparency maps (mode RGB) to add hollow or see-through effects. - Adjust surface roughness parameters: - **Intensity**: Higher value means rougher surface. - **Reflection Intensity**: Controls glossiness; higher value increases gloss. - Adjust metal density to apply metallic effect; 100% metal density shows full metal effect. - Reverse black/white areas if reflections appear inverted. --- ## Saving and Managing Materials - Save completed materials locally as ZFAB files for reuse. - Enter material name, structure, and other metadata in the Info area of the Property Editor before saving. - CLO’s material editor allows separate design and editing of PBR images. --- ## Material Editor Interface and Functions Key features of CLO’s material editor: - **Image Size**: Width and height settings; units can be changed; PPI sets image resolution. - **Transparency**: Toggle image transparency. - **Grid Display**: Option to show or hide grid. - **Circular Opacity**: Controls opacity of repeated images. - **Layer Management**: Add, select, duplicate, lock, delete, rename, reorder layers. - **Layer Blending**: Mix layers using various blend modes. - **Color Switching**: Change colors of specific areas in patterns by defining color blocks and replacing colors. Example: Blue-white gradient fabric colors changed to black and red using Color Switch. --- ## Printing and Pattern Integration in CLO - Prints can be added underneath fabric materials by importing print images. - Print display options include front, back, or both sides. - Print repeat types: flat, horizontal offset, vertical offset. - Prints can use the same PBR stickers as the fabric for realistic integration. - Print types can include metal effects. - Save prints along with fabrics as ZFAB files. --- ## Physical Fabric Attributes in CLO CLO includes over 70 built-in physical fabric attributes governing fabric behavior such as stretch and stiffness. - **Tensile Strength & Corner Line Strength**: Indicate stretch resistance. - High values = hard to stretch (denim, plain cotton). - Low values = easy to stretch (knitted fabric, thin silk). - **Bending Strength (Fabric Hardness)**: Controls stiffness. - High = stiff fabrics (denim, leather). - Low = soft fabrics (silk, soft flannel). - **Deformation Value**: Describes wrinkle shape.

chunks.content: --- ## Physical Fabric Attributes in CLO CLO includes over 70 built-in physical fabric attributes governing fabric behavior such as stretch and stiffness. - **Tensile Strength & Corner Line Strength**: Indicate stretch resistance. - High values = hard to stretch (denim, plain cotton). - Low values = easy to stretch (knitted fabric, thin silk). - **Bending Strength (Fabric Hardness)**: Controls stiffness. - High = stiff fabrics (denim, leather). - Low = soft fabrics (silk, soft flannel). - **Deformation Value**: Describes wrinkle shape. Users can preview different fabric types (denim, thick white fabric, knitted fabric) to observe wrinkle behavior and softness. --- ## CLO Fabric Versions and Simulation Improvements - **V1 Fabric**: Older version with basic physical property simulation. - **V2 Fabric**: Newer version with improved growth rate capturing nonlinear stretch behavior for more accurate simulation and scrolling. --- ## Additional Fabric Properties and Elastic Bands - Property Editor shows weight, friction coefficient, and thickness. - CLO includes presets for elastic bands like needle elastic band and shrink elastic band, selectable via the Attribute Editor. --- ## Measuring Fabric Physical Properties with CLO Tools - CLO offers a **fabric measuring device** and software tools to obtain accurate physical properties. - The **CLO Z-FAB Kit** is a scanning device that automates and improves accuracy in fabric digitization. - The **CLOF app** in CLO software supports physical property creation and editing, accessible via: - Object window fabric list (CLOF app button). - Fabric’s menu (three dots → Physical Properties). - Main menu with fabric selected. --- ## Using the CLOF App for Fabric Digitization - The CLOF app opens in the 2D window area; users can toggle between CLOF app and 2D window. - Enter fabric metadata: name, supplier, etc. - Access the CLOF app manual via the provided link. - Workflow: 1. Create a physical pattern. 2. Set physical properties. - Supports: - Direct scanning with CLOF Z-FAB Kit. - Importing scanned images from other devices. - If scanned files follow naming conventions, CLOF app auto-uploads corresponding PBR stickers. - Physical properties can be created or edited manually if no scanning device is available by entering fiber content, weight, and thickness. For detailed tutorials on CLOF Z-FAB usage, users can refer to additional video resources. --- This document provides the foundational knowledge and detailed workflows necessary for understanding and working with CLO fabrics, their textures, physical properties, and digital tools to create realistic virtual garments.

Combined with surface roughness to simulate metallic fabric effects. --- ## Creating Seamless PBR Stickers Two main methods to obtain seamless PBR stickers for CLO fabrics: 1. **Regular Scanners (e.g., Canon, Epson)** - Scan fabric textures, manually process seams in Photoshop, generate PBR stickers. 2. **Professional Scanners (e.g., WeZoo, Revolvet)** - Use specialized pattern processing software for automatic scanning and generation of PBR stickers with higher efficiency. --- ## Applying PBR Stickers in CLO Instructions for adding PBR stickers to fabric materials in CLO: - Open the Object window and select the material. - Use four small square icons next to each texture slot (texture, bump map, normal map, etc.) to add stickers. - Add all stickers at once by confirming the prompt or add selectively. - PBR sticker files must be named according to CLO’s material naming conventions and stored in a single folder. - CLO can **auto-create bump maps** (and other PBR maps) from base textures via an "auto-create" button. - Adjust bump map strength in the Attribute Editor; positive values enhance detail prominence, negative values invert the effect. --- ## Key Parameters for 3D Texture Effects Parameters controlling the 3D texture surface effects include: - **Height Range**: Maximum height of fabric surface peaks and valleys (e.g., white area = 3 mm height, black area = 5 mm depth). - **Offset**: Distance between the 3D grid and fabric surface. - **Height Cutoff**: Clips decal height below a threshold. - **Particle Size**: Size of particles in the 3D grid; smaller particles show more detail but increase file size and render time. - **Border Line Removal**: Ensures continuity by removing adjacent surface borders. Recommended settings for preview: Height Range = 3, Particle Size = 1. --- ## Previewing Fabric Effects in CLO - Use the render window to preview 3D textures and fabric details. - Drag and drop transparency maps (mode RGB) to add hollow or see-through effects. - Adjust surface roughness parameters: - **Intensity**: Higher value means rougher surface. - **Reflection Intensity**: Controls glossiness; higher value increases gloss. - Adjust metal density to apply metallic effect; 100% metal density shows full metal effect. - Reverse black/white areas if reflections appear inverted. --- ## Saving and Managing Materials - Save completed materials locally as ZFAB files for reuse. - Enter material name, structure, and other metadata in the Info area of the Property Editor before saving. - CLO’s material editor allows separate design and editing of PBR images. --- ## Material Editor Interface and Functions Key features of CLO’s material editor: - **Image Size**: Width and height settings; units can be changed; PPI sets image resolution. - **Transparency**: Toggle image transparency. - **Grid Display**: Option to show or hide grid. - **Circular Opacity**: Controls opacity of repeated images. - **Layer Management**: Add, select, duplicate, lock, delete, rename, reorder layers. - **Layer Blending**: Mix layers using various blend modes. - **Color Switching**: Change colors of specific areas in patterns by defining color blocks and replacing colors. Example: Blue-white gradient fabric colors changed to black and red using Color Switch. --- ## Printing and Pattern Integration in CLO - Prints can be added underneath fabric materials by importing print images. - Print display options include front, back, or both sides. - Print repeat types: flat, horizontal offset, vertical offset. - Prints can use the same PBR stickers as the fabric for realistic integration. - Print types can include metal effects. - Save prints along with fabrics as ZFAB files. --- ## Physical Fabric Attributes in CLO CLO includes over 70 built-in physical fabric attributes governing fabric behavior such as stretch and stiffness. - **Tensile Strength & Corner Line Strength**: Indicate stretch resistance. - High values = hard to stretch (denim, plain cotton). - Low values = easy to stretch (knitted fabric, thin silk). - **Bending Strength (Fabric Hardness)**: Controls stiffness. - High = stiff fabrics (denim, leather). - Low = soft fabrics (silk, soft flannel). - **Deformation Value**: Describes wrinkle shape. Users can preview different fabric types (denim, thick white fabric, knitted fabric) to observe wrinkle behavior and softness. --- ## CLO Fabric Versions and Simulation Improvements - **V1 Fabric**: Older version with basic physical property simulation. - **V2 Fabric**: Newer version with improved growth rate capturing nonlinear stretch behavior for more accurate simulation and scrolling. --- ## Additional Fabric Properties and Elastic Bands - Property Editor shows weight, friction coefficient, and thickness. - CLO includes presets for elastic bands like needle elastic band and shrink elastic band, selectable via the Attribute Editor. --- ## Measuring Fabric Physical Properties with CLO Tools - CLO offers a **fabric measuring device** and software tools to obtain accurate physical properties. - The **CLO Z-FAB Kit** is a scanning device that automates and improves accuracy in fabric digitization. - The **CLOF app** in CLO software supports physical property creation and editing, accessible via: - Object window fabric list (CLOF app button). - Fabric’s menu (three dots → Physical Properties). - Main menu with fabric selected. --- ## Using the CLOF App for Fabric Digitization - The CLOF app opens in the 2D window area; users can toggle between CLOF app and 2D window. - Enter fabric metadata: name, supplier, etc. - Access the CLOF app manual via the provided link. - Workflow: 1. Set physical properties. - Supports: - Direct scanning with CLOF Z-FAB Kit. - Importing scanned images from other devices. - If scanned files follow naming conventions, CLOF app auto-uploads corresponding PBR stickers. - Physical properties can be created or edited manually if no scanning device is available by entering fiber content, weight, and thickness.
